item.title: Powerful Nor’easter Bears Down on East Coast
item.description: A powerful nor'easter is bringing heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding to the Northeast, prompting states of emergency and flight cancellations.
item.content:encoded:
Rain, flooding and damaging winds are in the forecast for much of the coastal Northeast, including New York, Long Island and Boston.
More than a dozen counties in New York and New Jersey were under a state of emergency on Saturday morning as an intensifying nor’easter approached, threatening the nation’s most densely populated corridor with strong winds, heavy rain and flooding.
The center of the storm was forecast to linger along the New Jersey coast and move north toward Long Island through the weekend, before turning northeast early next week, the National Weather Service said in an advisory on Friday afternoon.
The Weather Service has issued coastal flood warnings effective until Sunday evening for northeast New Jersey, southeast New York and the Massachusetts coast, including Cape Cod and Nantucket. Up to three feet of flooding was forecast in waterfront areas in New Jersey and New York, with water levels likely to peak on Saturday morning.
Gusts stronger than 50 miles per hour were expected to hit eastern Long Island and southeastern New England, potentially causing power outages and felled trees, the Weather Service said. It also warned of dangerous rip currents and beach erosion.
The system is expected to linger offshore through the remainder of the weekend, potentially drifting farther west, said Frank Pereira, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service. It was still unclear how far west it would track, which would determine how much rain falls across the region.
Several airlines, including United, Delta, American and Southwest, have told customers to keep a close eye on the shifting forecast.
Here’s what else to know:
* Latest forecast: Meteorologists say the heavy rain could lead to some flash flooding, mainly in coastal Massachusetts, some of Rhode Island and eastern Long Island, where up to five inches of rain could fall this weekend. Though the tip of Long Island could see the brunt of the heavier rain and higher winds, significant rain could also fall toward the west, with potentially one to three inches across New York City, said Joe Pollina, a meteorologist with the Weather Service in New York City. * Coastal flooding: This is one the most certain threats, as the storm is developing during some of the highest tides of the month. As the storm moves north, strong winds, potentially above 45 miles per hour, could drive seawater toward the coast, producing waves up to 10 feet. * Rainfall total: The amount of rain will depend largely on the storm’s path. The most rainfall is expected along the coast, particularly over Cape Cod and eastern Long Island, but the threat of severe downpours stretches from Boston through New York City and down the Jersey Shore. High winds will be felt across areas at the coast. * El Niño effect: This is likely to be the first of several East Coast storms to follow this path over the next few months, driven by a developing El Niño weather pattern.
The Federal Aviation Authority is predicting delays at the major Northeast airports for any flights not canceled. The worst hit is Boston, where a ground stop is expected later in the day. At New York City and Philadelphia airports, a ground stop or delays are probable, the F.A.A. said. Even in Washington, D.C., it said, delays were possible.
Rain was pelting swaths of the East Coast early Saturday morning as the wind intensified and the storm inched closer to the Jersey shore. With wind gusts exceeding 50 m.p.h. lashing eastern Long Island and Cape Cod, and rain stretching from Philadelphia to Boston, the storm’s path is no longer in question among meteorologists. The only question now is: How long will it last? Expect a wet, windy weekend that will peak on Saturday but could linger into Monday.
The weather was already disrupting travel by early Saturday on the East Coast. More than 370 flights into or out of the country were canceled as of 6.a.m., according to the flight tracker FlightAware. Most had been set to go through airports in Massachusetts, including Boston Logan.
The East Coast of the United States hasn’t experienced a hurricane this year, but the storm trudging up the Northeast this weekend may feel like one in some places.
This storm is technically a nor’easter, a type of storm that more commonly stirs visions of heavy snow and plunging temperatures.
So what’s the difference, and why is this a nor’easter if it’s not going to snow?
“Nor’easter” applies broadly to storms that move along the Eastern Seaboard with winds that blow from the northeast. These types of storms typically occur between November and March. A nor’easter in September is relatively early, but not unheard of.
A nor’easter gets its energy from colliding air masses, like cold, dry air and warm, moist air. On satellite images, it often looks like a large comma. The long tail is the cold air wrapping around the storm’s center — that’s what causes thunderstorms to form — while the comma head is where the warm, moist air wraps around. These storms can be enhanced by the jet stream, a ribbon of very strong winds at the cruising altitude of commercial airplanes.
Often, the National Weather Service will avoid using the word “nor’easter” entirely if the storm doesn’t have a major snow component, because residents in the Northeast so strongly associate the term with snow. Dominic Ramunni, a meteorologist with the Weather Service in New York City, said that the local weather offices and the national centers of the Weather Service had a call Thursday and agreed to all use the same term for this storm so there wasn’t confusion in the media. So, they all began using nor’easter on Friday instead of coastal storm, because nor’easter was already being widely used.
Mr. Ramunni said that while weaker than some systems this past year in terms of precipitation and winds, the coastal flooding could rival some of the worst events in the past several years.
A hurricane is different: It is fueled by warm ocean temperatures and requires a calm atmosphere to intensify. At times, these storms can be hybrid versions that begin as hurricanes before morphing into more typical storms. A famous example is Hurricane Sandy, which started as a hurricane but then became what is called an extratropical storm — another name for a typical storm system found across the United States.
One way meteorologists monitor a storm’s strength is through its pressure. The lower the pressure, the more intense the storm.
Sandy reached an intensity of 940 millibars before it began to transition into an extratropical storm. That transition spread Sandy’s damaging winds out farther than they were as a hurricane. The storm surge had already built up over several days and pushed inland with hurricane force.
The storm was essentially a concoction of the worst hazards from both types of systems.
This weekend’s nor’easter is not Sandy. Its intensity is peaking around 992 millibars. (For context, a strong nor’easter this past February reached 965 millibars.) This doesn’t diminish this weekend’s potential for coastal erosion, strong winds and rainfall, but the Northeast coast has seen worse.
This storm isn’t even named, which is standard for anything other than a hurricane. Sandy only had a name because it was a hurricane first. The National Weather Service does not name winter storms.
In Europe, storms that could cause potential damage are routinely named. In the United States, some private organizations and media outlets choose to name winter storms unofficially.
On Friday morning, Mayor Zohran Mamdani warned on social media that the track of the nor’easter skirting the Atlantic seaboard had shifted closer to New York City, “bringing heavier rain and stronger winds.”
What that means for the metropolitan area is a blustery and wet weekend, with possible power outages and local flooding along the coast. Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency on Friday afternoon, telling residents to “take this storm seriously.”
A New York Yankees double header has been rescheduled and two major music festivals were canceled, including Global Citizen, a star-studded charity event that was walloped by extreme rain in 2023 and was to be held in Central Park on Saturday afternoon. The “All Things Go” festival, planned for Friday through Sunday at Forest Hills Stadium in Queens, was also canceled.
“Right now is your last chance to get ready before the nor’easter arrives,” city officials announced on Friday at 2 p.m. Coastal flood warnings are in place for all boroughs except for Manhattan, they said.
New Yorkers who live in low-lying areas should park their cars on higher ground, while all residents in the storm’s path should clear their storm drains and gutters, secure outdoor furniture and charge their devices, government officials said.
Coastal flooding — as much as three feet — could affect parts of Long Island and waterfront areas of Brooklyn, Queens, and the Bronx, as well as in South Queens and along the coast of New Jersey. For the worst of the flooding, look to high tides that roll in on Friday night at 7:30 p.m. and Saturday morning at 7:30 a.m. High tides will then hit the Bronx and northern Queens at midnight and noon, respectively. Waves in surf zones could reach up to 15 feet.
Rainfall is expected to be between three to five inches in Southern Connecticut and Long Island, and between 1.5 to 3 inches across the city and up to four inches along the Jersey shoreline.
Brian Ciemnecki, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service, said that the rain won’t fall all at once, so the risk of flash flooding remains low. “We’re looking at a longer term event,” he said. It will rain off and on from Friday night into Sunday morning, he said.
Perhaps the most pronounced element of the nor’easter will be the wind.
“We’re already starting to see strong winds across the area,” Mr. Ciemnecki said early Friday afternoon. But wind gusts will strengthen into the afternoon and evening, and could reach speeds of up to 55 miles per hour across Long Island and 50 miles per hour in New York City.
With strong winds comes the threat of downed trees and power lines, which means power outages and blocked roadways, officials warned.
Currently, there are 5,675 workers across New York State who are on standby for making repairs and clearing debris, including more than 300 contractors secured by Con Edison, according to Gov. Kathy Hochul’s office and the power utility.
“I urge New Yorkers to stay informed, stay prepared, and closely monitor local weather updates as conditions develop over the weekend,” Ms. Hochul said.
New Yorkers can sign up for the city and state alert systems NotifyNYC and New York Alert, while New York City and New Jersey residents can follow @NotifyNYC and @ReadyNJ accounts on all major social media platforms.
The National Weather Service plans to release another update on Friday at 6 p.m.
It was raining. That was what first startled Alyssa Atwood when she stepped off the plane on Christmas Island in August.
Torrential downpours had already turned the dirt roads into impassable waterways, leaving her research team questioning whether their trucks could even reach their lodge.
When she finally waded into the Pacific Ocean, it wasn’t quite as she remembered it.
“You almost don’t want to wear a wet suit, it’s so hot,” said Dr. Atwood, a paleoclimate scientist at Florida State University who recently returned from the island, a remote coral atoll that sits in the Central Pacific at the geographical bull’s-eye of El Niño.
The typical winter peak of El Niño is months away. Yet on Christmas Island, also known as Kiritimati, the ocean was already at least two degrees warmer than average, hovering between 30 and 30.5 degrees Celsius, and the reef was actively bleaching. It was an ominous sign of what forecast models suggest could become a record-breaking El Niño, and stark proof that the ocean had already entered uncharted territory amid what some have called a “super El Niño” or even a “Godzilla El Niño.”
It has already helped make this the hottest summer on record in the United States and boosted Pacific hurricane activity with rare, damaging storms near Hawaii. At the same time, it has kept hurricanes away from the Atlantic, making parts of the Caribbean drier than usual. And as winter approaches, experts are closely monitoring what El Niño’s most intense phase will mean for the day-to-day weather.
The dire warnings may leave everyday people around the world with a central question: How concerned should they be?
## Who gets more rain? Who gets less?
First, a brief explanation: El Niño is a natural weather pattern that comes around every few years. It typically develops in the spring or summer, gets stronger through the fall, and peaks in the winter. It doesn’t, by itself, mean a wetter winter in California or a warmer Christmas in New York, but more often than not, when El Niño arrives, that’s what tends to happen. A stronger El Niño like this one can make it more likely.
Emily Becker, a climate scientist at the University of Miami, explained that seasonal forecasts, like the ones making headlines as the off-the-charts scale of this year’s pattern became clear, represent shifting probabilities rather than precise predictions. A winter forecast can offer a strong signal that December, January and February will likely be above or below average, she said, but not when a single storm will hit and how bad it will be.
Think of the El Niño pattern as a dance between the ocean and the atmosphere. As winds in the tropical Pacific weaken, a pool of warm water that otherwise would have stayed in the western Pacific near Indonesia instead sloshes east, dragging the ocean’s primary zone of thunderstorm activity with it. This shift acts like a boulder dropped into a stream, rippling upward through the atmosphere to alter the jet stream and disrupt weather patterns worldwide.
“I see El Niño as an artist that is providing some broad-brush preliminary sketches on what to expect for upcoming seasons,” said Michelle L’Heureux, an El Niño expert at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. “But the details of the final portrait will be determined by events we cannot predict months in advance.”
California, being on the Pacific, is often the first land mass affected by this new pattern. The state gets most of its annual precipitation in the winter, so an El Niño year leads to the kind of storms that live on in popular memory for decades. That’s what happened in 1997, when relentless storms left more than a dozen people dead and caused a half-billion dollars in damage.
But while a strong El Niño loads the dice, it does not offer a guarantee.
In 2015, another “Godzilla El Niño” year, forecasters expected winter storms to help break a multiyear megadrought. But the storms were forced around California by more regional weather patterns.
“Our return interval in California is two-thirds,” Dr. Becker said. In other words, California sees above-average rainfall in only two out of every three El Niño seasons. So there’s a one-in-three chance that the winter stays dry.
This time around, weather experts believe California is more likely to end up with more rain, said Jon Gottschalck, who works at NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center. But that forecast is based on the similar statistics used in 2015, and even Mr. Gottschalck cautions that California is often more difficult to predict with certainty than other parts of the country during El Niño.
Parts of the South, too, are likely to end up with more rain this winter, Mr. Gottschalck said. The jet stream routinely pins itself across the southern United States during El Niño, delivering a steady conveyor belt of Pacific moisture across Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas.
That could be a good thing, said Weston Anderson, a crop scientist.
“This El Niño may actually bring some needed relief to the area, with increased precipitation in the Southern U.S.,” Dr. Anderson said, noting that winter wheat crops in Kansas and Oklahoma stand to benefit significantly after years of La Niña-driven drought.
Unlike in California, the signal El Niño provides for above-average winter rainfall across the Gulf Coast, the Southeast and up the Eastern Seaboard of the United States is among the most reliable seasonal forecasters can read.
“The probability there’s pretty high,” said Ben Kirtman, a climate scientist at the University of Miami.
## What if you’re in the Northeast? It’s complicated.
While it’s extremely likely that there will be more storms, and that they will move up the East Coast as they do every winter, those systems don’t always translate into snowfall as they move into the Northeast, as they might in a year without El Niño.
Why? Because the northern half of the United States leans toward significantly warmer temperatures during El Niño. That means potential snowstorms often shift into rain or ice in the major Northeast cities, because it’s not always cold enough for snow to fall or accumulate.
“There’s a reasonably strong relationship between El Niño and a warmer winter throughout the northern tier,” Dr. Becker said.
But don’t put your winter coat back in the attic quite yet. A generally warm northern winter does not rule out sudden, severe blasts of Arctic cold.
Amy Butler, a research scientist at NOAA’s Chemical Sciences Laboratory, explained that El Niño frequently triggers what weather people call “sudden stratospheric warmings” high above the North Pole. These warmings can push the cold Arctic air farther south.
If you’re in New York, for example, it wouldn’t be impossible to be enjoying a warmer than usual Christmas Eve, only to need that heavy parka by the time the New Year rolls around.
## This El Niño may enter uncharted territory.
As global temperatures continue to break records, scientists are grappling with how climate change, caused primarily by the burning of fossil fuels, is altering El Niño itself.
“El Niños have been acting like a stair step,” said Dr. Kim Cobb, a climate scientist at Brown. Global temperatures tend to spike during an El Niño, and when the cycle winds down, temperatures drop — only never back to the previous baseline. “That’s what frightens me about El Niño,” she said.
Dr. Cobb works with Dr. Atwood on Christmas Island, where they are watching corals bleaching before El Niño has even reached its winter stride. Super El Niños are recurring on tighter timelines, and fragile ecosystems no longer have sufficient time to recover between shocks.
That acceleration concerns her. “People should be planning for worst-case scenarios,” she said.
Dr. Michael McPhaden, the director of a NOAA buoy network that has monitored El Niño conditions since the 1990s, offers a different framing.
“Ignorance is the foundation of fear,” he said. “El Niño should not be feared. It should be understood for what it does, what it can do, and what you can do to prepare for it.”
That preparation is being tested like never before. Historical statistical models are fed data on past El Niño patterns to predict how the next one will behave. They have struggled to keep up with the extreme heat of the ocean this year.
There’s another type of projection, called a dynamic physical model, which calculates atmospheric physics based on current data rather than relying on past examples. Those models are forecasting a much stronger, more disruptive El Niño period.
“We are very much in uncharted territory,” Dr. Kirtman said. “What I feel completely confident in is that things are going to happen that are entirely unanticipated — things we didn’t even think of.”
An unusual early fall nor’easter is expected to deliver a slate of weather hazards over the weekend, with coastal areas of New York City and Long Island at particular risk of flooding. Some areas of eastern Long Island could also see more than three inches of rain, while totals over an inch will be more widespread.
Meteorologists said that high winds, choppy seas and the coincidence of a storm surge with the abnormally high tides that accompany Saturday’s full moon were likely to produce waves of up to 10 feet, rip currents and beach erosion all along the Eastern Seaboard through Sunday evening.
As with any forecast, however, there is still uncertainty about how much rain will ultimately fall in New York City, but the National Weather Service has said that the area is looking at a slight risk of “excessive rainfall.”
New York City’s sewers and subways, which were built more than 100 years ago, were not designed for the fast and furious deluges that have become routine with climate change. Many of the roadways surrounding the city, where storm water tends to pool during these extreme rainfall events, are low lying and were built over wetlands.
By the end of this century, the city could see 150 percent more days with more than an inch of rain. Nuisance flooding and waterlogged commutes — and the headaches that come with them — are becoming the new normal, along with life-threatening flash flood events.
Here’s how New Yorkers can prepare.
## Why does it flood every time it rains?
As New York grows hotter because of global warming, the atmosphere is able to hold more moisture, which means heavier downpours.
Most of New York City’s sewer and drainage network is designed to manage a maximum capacity of 1.75 inches of rainfall per hour. When extreme weather or “cloudbursts” drop more, the system becomes rapidly overwhelmed, leading to street and basement flooding.
It is easy to forget that New York City is coastal. It sits near the Atlantic Ocean and is cut through with several brackish rivers that rise and fall with the tides. As climate change increases sea levels, which then push up groundwater tables, the earth underneath our buildings, streets and sidewalks will be less able to absorb the water that pools beneath them.
This means that storm water will drain more slowly and contribute to flooding, particularly in low-lying and subterranean areas, like basements and subway stations. Parts of the subway system, including much of Manhattan’s west side, are below the groundwater table, requiring the Metropolitan Transportation Authority to pump about 14 million gallons of water a day from the tunnels, even during dry weather.
## Look out for weather warnings.
Government officials encourage all New Yorkers to sign up for the city and state alert systems, NotifyNYC and New York Alert.
The alerts announce extreme rain, roadway closures and flash flood watches and warnings. Warnings are the more serious of the two. If you receive such an alert, it means that flooding is imminent and that you should follow official guidance immediately. This could include moving to higher ground if you are in a basement apartment or a low-lying area. The National Weather Service also updates local forecasts throughout the day and night.
## What if my subway station is flooded?
First things first: Straphangers should bookmark the M.T.A. website or download its app. The authority provides updates in real time about train delays and stoppages, as well as the reasons behind them, along with information on alternate routes.
During extreme rainfall, excess water can enter the system from the street, from underground and from backed‑up storm drains.
Though recent videos on social media have shown waterfalls on train tracks and storm water gushing down subway entrances, a spokesman for the M.T.A. said flooding in the subway is still rare.
But passengers who find themselves in such a situation should listen to announcements and follow the instructions of station personnel and train crews, the spokesman said. When leaving flooded areas, passengers should use the handrails near the exits for support and move slowly, he added. More guidance around flooding and public transit can be found here.
## Do not drive on roads covered in water.
Many cars can be swept away in just one or two feet of flooding.
“The guidance is simple: Turn around, don’t drown,” said Aries Dela Cruz, a spokesman for the city’s Office of Emergency Management. “You cannot reliably tell how deep the water is, how fast it is moving or whether the road beneath it has been damaged or washed away.”
The floodwaters could also be covering dangerous debris, electrical hazards or other risks, he added.
If you do find yourself stuck, roll down your window, get out of the car immediately and move to higher ground — perhaps onto the car’s roof — and call 911. Step-by-step instructions for how to escape a car in floodwaters can be found here.
## Which areas are prone to flooding?
“If you live near water, in a low-lying area or near city storm drains, you are on the front lines of flooding,” said Dominic Ramunni, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service. New Yorkers can learn more about their flood risks by plugging their locations into the city’s storm water map.
In New York City, basement and ground-level apartments are especially at risk. When signing up for NotifyNYC, residents can select a special basement apartment alert option to receive additional guidance for extreme rainfall.
Water flows downhill, so if you are in an area that dips, is at the bottom of the hill or along the coast, chances are that you will experience flooding. And since New York City is covered in asphalt, it lacks the porousness of natural areas with soil, which can ease drainage. This means that flooding can crop up anywhere when infrastructure becomes overwhelmed or storm drains become clogged.
The nonprofit Rebuild by Design offers an interactive flood map based on 311 data it has collected. The map invites New Yorkers to share their flooding stories, including video. Visitors to the site can click around to find out which neighborhoods have been hardest hit by which kind of flooding, such as clogged storm drains or basement water.
Knowing and understanding the geography of where you live and work is helpful. The website Welikia.org shows what the city used to look like before it was developed, including where marshes and streams once sat. If you live atop a paved-over wetland, swamp or body of water, it could be prone to flooding.
## Have a plan before the rain begins.
Many neighborhoods have community groups, some on Facebook, that monitor and organize around extreme weather. Sign up and get involved.
Install a flood sensor in your basement. You can get one for free every spring and summer, when the city’s Department of Environmental Protection holds flood preparation town halls in low-lying neighborhoods. After the sessions, officials distribute the free sensors, as well as free pumps and inflatable flood barriers.
In the hours leading up to a storm, residents should try to clear storm drains of trash and vegetation. Though the city cleans storm drains, debris can accumulate fast, and there is only so much territory that workers can cover at the last minute. New York City Emergency Management offers a guide for flood preparation here.
Finally, if you live in a low-lying area and the forecast looks particularly dangerous, arrange to stay with friends or family members, or at a shelter or hotel on higher ground. Develop a plan, including a go bag, so you can leave your home quickly. NotifyNYC and city leadership will often announce which shelters are open during dangerous weather events.
Max Bearak contributed reporting.

item.title: Roads flood in New Jersey, homes inundated as nor’easter take shape
item.description: A powerful nor'easter is causing widespread flooding and power outages across the Northeastern U.S., leading to evacuations and cancellations.
item.content:encoded:
More than 70,000 customers were without electricity in the U.S. Northeast on Saturday, the sign of a powerful nor’easter expected to create dangerous conditions through the weekend. Forecasters warned of gale winds that could down trees and heavy inundations that could put roads underwater.
Tens of millions of people are in the path of the storm already beginning to lash the region with strong winds and rain as the region braces for much more. Dangerous flooding is expected along the Mid-Atlantic coast, particularly near New Jersey and Delaware, according to the National Weather Service.
“This storm is expected to bring major coastal flooding to the Mid-Atlantic Coast over multiple high tide cycles through the weekend,” the weather service said Saturday. “Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses.”
In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, water, with waves rippling along its surface, flooded the streets, inundating some homes. About 34 miles (54.7 kilometers) up the coast in the borough of Manasquan, where some roads were also flooding, Mayor Mike Mangan said he expected “a lot of water in the streets for a long time.” A voluntary evacuation had been issued earlier in some low-lying areas of the community.
Concerts were canceled, along with dozens of flights going into airports in Boston, Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard on Friday and Saturday. Several airlines were offering to waive some change or cancellation fees for some East Coast flights through the weekend.
Brian Kelly, the mayor of the tiny New Jersey beach community Sea Bright, said the borough is bracing for winds up to 50 mph (80 kph) and flooding that could reach up to 6 feet (1.8 meters) on some streets. Officials expect the flooding to start Saturday and worsen by midday.
“It’s going to be worse than average. We do have probably one or two flooding events a year, sometimes more, sometimes less, but I think this one will be closer to an Irene-scale flooding event,” Kelly said, referencing the 2011 storm that caused major flooding in the Northeast. “I hope I’m wrong, but that’s my gut feeling.”
Kelly hopes hundreds of residents living in low-lying areas will consider evacuating. He said the town will open its recreation center for evacuees.
Peak wind gusts could approach 60 to 65 mph (97 to 105 kph) on Cape Cod, Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket on Friday night and Saturday, compared with about 50 to 55 mph (80 to 89 kph) around Boston and 35 to 40 mph (56 to 64 kph) farther inland, according to Matthew Belk, a meteorologist with NWS in Norton, Massachusetts.
“It’s definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you’re likely to see,” Belk said.
Belk said nor’easters are not unusual as New England moves into fall, but one concern this early in the season is that leaves remain on the trees, creating more wind resistance. That could increase the risk of downed limbs, which in turn can cause power outages and leave debris in roads, he said.
Along the Atlantic coasts of New Jersey and Delaware, wind gusts could reach 60 mph (96.6 kph), according to NWS. In southeastern Connecticut and eastern Long Island, New York, gusts could get almost as high, potentially downing tree limbs and power lines.
### Storm disrupts concerts, baseball and flights
More than 200 flights to and from airports in Boston, Nantucket, Martha’s Vineyard and New York had been canceled Friday, and more cancellations were already in place for Saturday.
Meanwhile, the Red Sox announced their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs would be adjusted. The team moved the Sunday afternoon game to Friday to create a split doubleheader. Separately, Ed Sheeran announced that his high-profile Friday and Saturday shows at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, would be canceled due to the storm.
The public ferry service connecting Cape Cod with the islands of Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard was experiencing widespread cancellations Friday due to strong winds and choppy water.
In Rhode Island, ferries were also canceled for Block Island. The disrupted ferry service was expected to also spill into Saturday.
For people who regularly travel to and from the islands, the possibility of getting stuck on one side or the other is “part of life,” said Sean Driscoll, a spokesperson for the Woods Hole, Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket Steamship Authority. Most people have backup plans in place for when boats are canceled.
“It’s a nuisance, but you know, we know what to do with this kind of stuff at this point,” he said. “This is not out of the realm of ordinary.”
Ashley Destino of Gloucester, a coastal city in northern Massachusetts, enjoyed a stroll along the beach with her two young children before preparing to hunker down at home during the storm.
“We came to the beach on Friday afternoon because we knew we were going to be inside all weekend,” said Destino, who has Legos and arts and crafts activities prepared to entertain her two children, ages 7 and 4.
She also prepared by securing her boat with additional lines, and her husband pulled out a generator in case the electricity goes out.
Willingham reported from Boston. Associated Press writers Michael Casey in Boston; Rodrique Ngowi in Gloucester, Massachusetts; and Anthony Izaguirre in New York contributed to this report.

item.title: Princess Diana considered becoming first lady after American politician courted her, brother claims
item.description: A new memoir by Princess Diana's brother reveals her post-divorce aspirations, including becoming a US First Lady, and provides new details about King Charles's reactions to her death.
item.content:encoded:
Charles Spencer's new memoir Swan Song details Princess Diana's private hopes after her divorce, including a dream of becoming American first lady, and startling conversations with King Charles surrounding her death.
Charles Spencer's new memoir Swan Song reveals that Princess Diana once considered becoming American first lady after her divorce. The book also details startling conversations with then-Prince Charles surrounding her death.
Spencer wrote that one of Diana's many powerful aging American suitors, keen to secure her as the ultimate trophy wife, had told her he was sure to win the presidency if she married him. Diana asked her brother if he thought she would make a good American first lady. He said Diana was more titillated by the idea of living in the White House than by the prospect of marrying the would-be elderly husband.
Diana's White House Ambitions
She had a mischievous attraction to reinventing herself in a role that would make her enemies in the British Royal Family sick with jealousy, while ushering in an era of glamour in the White House that would surely have surpassed even that of the Jackie Kennedy years. The memoir, titled Swan Song, also covers Charles' reaction to Diana's death.
Spencer wrote that on the morning Diana died, then-Prince Charles sounded giddily elated - like a lottery winner, he remembered thinking at the time. In hindsight, Spencer wrote, he believed that Charles' first reaction to her death was that it likely freed him up to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not.
He also wrote that while they were arguing over funeral arrangements, Charles told him, Rest assured … we'll forget her soon enough! Spencer said he was stunned for a few seconds before responding, I can't believe you just said that, before hanging up. Earlier in their conversation, Spencer wrote that Charles accused the Spencer family of having no sense of duty because Spencer had objected to Princess Diana's funeral arrangements.
Charles Reaction to Diana Death
Spencer wrote that he believed the diatribe was the result of Charles' pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. A statement from the palace said, While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss.
Spencer wrote that after falling in love with heart surgeon Dr. Hasnat Khan following her divorce, Diana had the naïve yet impossible dream of moving to South Africa - where Spencer lived at the time - with her boyfriend because England had become intolerable to her. Might they, she dared hope, move there together, and carve out a life? he wrote.
He said she dreamed that Khan could work at a hospital in Cape Town, and they could live happily - normally - nearby her brother. Despite Panorama reporter Martin Bashir allegedly telling Diana a series of falsehoods, including that she was being surveilled by MI6, that Charles was unwittingly bugging her through a device on his watch and that her children's nanny had aborted Prince Charles' child after an affair, Diana almost canceled the interview, Spencer said.
Persuading Diana for Panorama Interview
But Bashir and the show's executive producer persisted, Spencer wrote. He said they arranged a clandestine meeting in a parking garage, where Spencer believes they persuaded Diana that her life was in imminent danger and that doing the interview was the best way to protect herself.
Spencer said he had a conversation with Charles after his own father's funeral, during which Charles told him he was lucky his father had died because he got to inherit when he was so young. Charles allegedly said that while Spencer was inheriting his ancestral home of Althorp in his 20s, the prince complained that he was 43 and employed 50 people, but my parents insist on treating me like - like a child!
Spencer also wrote that Diana told him early in her relationship with the prince that the queen had once considered having Charles' ears pinned back because their protrusion had caused him to be teased at school and mocked by the media. Prince Philip put a stop to it, however, according to Spencer. Spencer said he found the claim improbable, but didn't press her for more information because he was focused on the realization that she was ending her marriage.
Harry Movie Project Sparks Tension
The memoir also addresses Prince Harry's reported Princess Diana movie project, which is sparking controversy. A reported movie about Princess Diana spearheaded by Prince Harry for the 30th anniversary of her passing is causing royal family tension. Johnny Joey Jones reacted with a theory about Markle acting as an American plant to dismantle the monarchy, sparking laughs from the co-hosts. Experts say the rumored film might feel like another betrayal to Prince William as the rift grows.
The book also reveals that Princess Diana never forgave Sarah Ferguson for one betrayal that ended their friendship. Another revelation covers Princess Diana's honeymoon letter, which reveals a young bride playing with grown-ups in the royal family. The memoir also touches on Princess Diana and JFK Jr.'s secret meeting that fueled romance rumors for decades.
Additionally, an investigator said Princess Diana could have survived the fatal Paris crash if she made one simple choice.

item.title: The frat omertà: Whistleblower warns of ‘code of silence’ after Ole Miss deaths, alleged Penn State coke ring
item.description: A former fraternity member warns of a "code of silence" enabling dangerous hazing and drug rings in Greek organizations, citing recent incidents at Ole Miss and Penn State.
item.content:encoded:
Andrew Lohse, a former Dartmouth fraternity member and hazing survivor, says a code of silence enables dangerous hazing and drug rings after two Ole Miss student deaths and an alleged Penn State cocaine distribution operation.
A former Ivy League fraternity member is warning that a code of silence inside Greek organizations enables dangerous hazing and drug rings. Andrew Lohse, a 36-year-old hazing survivor and author of Confessions of an Ivy League Frat Boy, spoke out after two Ole Miss student deaths and an alleged Penn State cocaine distribution ring.
You need a code of omerta if you are trying to create an organization that is essentially like a criminal organization, Lohse told Fox News Digital. He was talking about fraternities and the culture that he says punishes whistleblowers. Lohse was a brother at Sigma Alpha Epsilon at Dartmouth. For years and years, the last 10 years, it is like whenever someone dies in a frat, that is when my phone rings, Lohse said.
Ole Miss Deaths And Penn State Cocaine Ring
He said recent headlines immediately reminded him of his own time as a brother. The Ole Miss cases and the Penn State allegations both involve young men in fraternity settings. One of the Ole Miss students found dead this past week was Ryan Strang, a Phi Delta Theta fraternity brother. He was found at an off-campus home.
Authorities found packages of kratom, a commercially available drug derided as gas station heroin, at both death scenes. Its role in either death was not immediately clear. The fraternity said in a statement that the loss of two young lives is a profound tragedy. Phi Delta Theta joins the University of Mississippi and the broader Ole Miss community in mourning Robert and Aidan Hamilton, the statement said.
The fraternity extended deepest sympathies to family, friends, chapter brothers, classmates and all who knew them. These losses reinforce the importance of a collective commitment to health, safety and well-being on college campuses today, the fraternity said. It encouraged the Phi Delta Theta community to keep the Strang family, the Mississippi Alpha Chapter and everyone affected in their thoughts. Phi Delta Theta has not been accused of any wrongdoing.
Ole Miss toxicology reports are expected soon, and an official said results may trigger an anti-fentanyl law. The university has named the students found dead as an official addressed the potential for foul play. The kratom packages recovered at two sites remain under investigation. At Penn State, prosecutors allege in court documents that pledges were coerced into cutting and packaging cocaine as part of an alleged organized drug ring.
Penn State Cocaine Ring Charges And Criminal Behavior
Agostino Abbateillo, 24, is one of 14 men charged with operating a massive cocaine ring near Penn State's campus. The case has drawn national attention. Lohse said when he read that pledges were in the background doing that, he thought it was sort of amazing, but in a bad way, and also extremely brazen. He said the alleged conduct shows how fraternities can normalize criminal behavior.
He urged incoming college students to carefully weigh the downside risks before pledging. Dangers like kratom did not exist when Lohse was in school, he said. There was no kratom, no tranq, no smoking bath salts, no fentanyl, Lohse said. Back then, the cocaine was more or less just cocaine.
It was not like every time somebody did cocaine they could die. Separately, police in Madison, Wisconsin, said they found roughly 30 partially clothed young men packed inside a sweltering basement. The men were covered in food, condiments and other liquids, and several pledges showed signs of being physically assaulted. Officers were dispatched to the Alpha Epsilon Pi house on Wednesday night and are investigating the alleged hazing.
AEPi Denounces Hazing Allegations
AEPi Headquarters takes the allegations involving our Pi Chapter in Madison, Wisconsin, extremely seriously, said Jonathan Pierce, the fraternity's chief communications officer. We will cooperate fully with the authorities investigating this matter. Hazing is a betrayal of everything our fraternity stands for. There is no place for it in AEPi.
No exceptions. No excuses. Lohse said the recent headlines represent a sad moment for society and civilization. These organizations should be forces of good, he said.
Young men need it more than ever. Young men are more adrift than ever, there is no moral leadership. He described a vacuum in the center of higher education and American society that used to be filled by God, religion and the church. He said it is totally vacant now.
Lohse Details Sigma Alpha Epsilon Hazing Rituals
During his time as a brother at Sigma Alpha Epsilon, Lohse said he was forced to swim in a kiddie pool full of vomit while being urinated on. He said he was forced to chug vinegar or milk to the point that he and his fellow pledge brothers would vomit in a room covered with tarps. He also said he was forced into a small basement crawl space for a period of time. He described constant coerced indoctrination rituals.
Lohse said he believes a code of omerta, or silence, protects those who run dangerous pledge activities and drug operations. He said the pattern repeats when deaths or arrests occur. He wants students and parents to understand the risks before joining. The Ole Miss deaths remain under investigation, with toxicology results pending.
The Penn State case involves 14 defendants and allegations of pledge involvement in cocaine cutting and packaging. The Madison hazing investigation is ongoing, and AEPi has pledged full cooperation. Lohse said the common thread is a culture that puts loyalty to the group above safety and law. He said fraternities can be forces for good, but only if they reject secrecy and abuse. He said young men need moral leadership, not criminal-style codes.

item.title: Starlink is launching gigabit download speeds for existing users as fees may rise
item.description: Starlink will introduce gigabit download speeds for maritime business clients by December and for land-based businesses in 2027, with potential price increases.
item.content:encoded:
Starlink will deliver gigabit downloads from its satellite network in 2026, just as promised, but the blazing speeds will first be available to owners of its most expensive equipment.
According to the memo that Starlink sent to enterprise clients, those Business Maritime plan users who paid $1,999 for its latest Performance Kit and are paying a monthly fee of at least $250 for the lowest 50 GB tier would enjoy doubling of their speeds by the end of December.
In short, Starlink customers bobbing around on ships and yachts could soon see download speeds nudging toward 1 Gbps as long as they own the Performance Gen 3 terminal, but their monthly bill may grow along with their bandwidth. The current spec sheet lists that dish at 475 Mbps down and 75 Mbps up, essentially the same as those of the Standard Kit that goes for $349 on Amazon, so doubling the download side would put maritime connections close to gigabit territory indeed.
Land-based business customers will reportedly get gigabit speeds in 2027 as the timing lines up with SpaceX's V3 satellite deployment roadmap. The company is targeting Monday for the Starship Flight 14 launch, which is expected to carry a batch of V3 satellites into orbit. As big as a Boeing 737 when their solar panels are unfurled, the V3 satellites offer 10x the throughput of the current V2 kit but need to be shot up with SpaceX's giant Starship rocket that is still undergoing test flights.
Elon Musk has previously said that the V3 constellation needs to reach serious numbers before Starlink can flip the gigabit switch broadly. Just the small inaugural batch it will launch on September 28 will add 3% capacity to the whole Starlink satellite Internet network.
There, however, might be some pricing shifts on the way as Starlink is apparently renaming its Local Priority and Global Priority tiers to Business Plan and Global Business Plan starting December 1, alongside a UK price hike and a new cap limiting Business Plan users to 30 days of service outside their home region before they get pushed onto the costlier Global tier.
Starlink already charges up to $2,150 a month for its top 2 TB business plan at today's 400 Mbps peak speeds, yet it wouldn't be surprising if faster maritime throughput arrived with some kind of new pricing structure attached. The V3 satellites will bring a drastic 24x boost in uploads as well, though the up to 160 Gbps bandied about may not materialize right away with the first batch that is just about to be launched.
Source(s)
Tim Belfall via PCMag

item.title: They survived the worst —and they have an urgent message for a shaken America
item.description: An activist discusses his updated book, which uses historical examples of resistance to inspire hope in the face of political despair, particularly regarding current American political challenges.
item.content:encoded:
When I think about "the impossible," at least in terms of modern American politics, I think of stopping President Donald Trump's attempts to become a dictator. Thanks to his aggressive attempts to rig the 2026 midterm elections and Democrats' wimpy response to those efforts, countless concerned citizens suspect as I do that America's days as a democracy may soon end.
Yet if you visit theimpossible.org, you'll find a website promoting a book with an antidote to this despair.
In his book "The Impossible Will Take a Little While," longtime social justice activist Paul Loeb — whose career spans back to protesting the Vietnam War and opposing President Ronald Reagan's nuclear arms buildup — Loeb updates a text originally published in 2004 to inspire citizen activists. Spanning the entire globe, Loeb profiles individuals like Nelson Mandela, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate and South Africa's first democratically elected president who was persecuted for opposing apartheid; Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., another Nobel Peace Prize laureate who led the American civil rights movement; Václav Havel, a dissident playwright who eventually became the first president of the Czech Republic; and Alexei Navalny, Russian opposition leader who died in an Arctic prison.
Through these stories, Loeb argues that ordinary citizens can feel empowered even at a time that feels impossibly demoralizing.
This interview has been lightly edited for clarity, context and length.
Hope in Trump's America.
ROZSA: First, you wrote in your book that "hope seems more beleaguered now than at any other point in my lifetime." What made you decide to update the book, and how did that sense of urgency shape the new voices that you added, such as Alexei Navalny [the critic of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin who mysteriously died], Jungmin Choi [from South Korea's lightstick protests] and Andrew Carter [who covered Chicago's anti-ICE protests]?
LOEB: Yeah, that's a really good question. So what happened was when Trump was reelected, I was like, God, people are rightly just demoralized, overwhelmed, scared, just feeling like things are gonna be terrible, which it turned out was true. [laughs] Sometimes you anticipate things and you overreact, and I don't think people's reaction once Trump was elected was an overreaction. It was accurate that things were really gonna get bad. And so I thought, well, I don't want people to give up, because if they give up, we're just really screwed. So I've got this book that's really helpful, but I think the last edition had come out in 2014. So it's an old book, and some of it, particularly the introductions, felt like they were kind of part of that time.
And so I asked the publisher, and she said, "We could try and get books in the stores now, but honestly, let's just really update it." And so I jumped in, and what I was trying to do was really do two things. One is keep stories that, to my mind, may be older stories, but they're really important ones. So understanding what it was like for Nelson Mandela to be in jail for 27 years and still find ways to resist — that doesn't date. I read that today, and something bad happens with Trump, and I'm like, okay, yeah, this is bad, but other people have gone through hard situations as well. Or in challenging the communist dictatorships in Czechoslovakia. So there's stories that are the same.
And then I thought, okay, well, what do I wanna add? And I wanted to add some that were just contemporary. So literally, Trump gets elected in November, and in December the South Korean president decides to become a dictator and starts a coup. Because the rules said that the parliament could overturn martial law, he sends the soldiers to the parliament to drag the parliamentarians out so they don't have a quorum and prevent them from blocking his martial law. And what happened is that thousands and thousands of ordinary South Koreans just surrounded the building, blocked the soldiers, and — because it was the middle of the night — helped the people in parliament who came in to vote on it climb over the walls.
You had soldiers doing things like — my favorite one is a bunch of them were deployed and they stopped for ramen noodles instead. [laughs] It's like, "Hey, we've got orders, but we're kind of hungry, let's stop for ramen noodles." And another one used bureaucratic rules and prohibited a military helicopter from taking off. The top generals were all with the coup, but the junior officers said, "You know what? We're gonna go, but we're gonna stay in the military buses. We're not gonna go over to the parliament." So you had this broad resistance, and then it continued. By the morning, they negated the coup, but then the call was to impeach President Yoon, and eventually — he's now been tried and is in prison, along with the officials who went along with the coup.
So I looked at that story and I thought, for sadly obvious reasons [laughs], this is a very relevant contemporary story. And so I just took quite a bit of time, looked around at who's writing about it. Finally found a piece in a great little online magazine called Waging Nonviolence. It was written right after the first days of it, so I worked with the author to update it. And that piece actually leads off the new edition after my introduction.
Navalny is interesting — you mentioned him — because at first glance, you wouldn't think that a story about somebody who died in Putin's prison was gonna be a good fit for a book on political hope. But a friend who works for a great activist organization kind of said exactly that to me. She said, "Look, I know this isn't gonna be obvious, but I just finished reading the book. If you read the book, it's gonna give you hope." And I did. And what was interesting there is — how to describe it? Navalny has this amazing strength of will, but also this gallows humor. So he's writing and he's in prison and he's saying, "Hey, somebody must have read George Orwell's 1984 and thought, 'Cool, guys, we could do something like this.'" And he's just, "Oh, there's somebody next to my bed all night waking me up. They're so concerned about my welfare and that I'm not gonna accidentally wander away." And so you read it and you feel this spirit fighting back. And when I ended up reading it, I was like, "Well, okay, this gives me courage to fight back." So that's an example.
There's a great poet who I'd never heard of, a young woman — she died last year of cancer — named Andrea Gibson. I live in Seattle, and I was watching this beautiful aerialist performance by the waterfront. And the background to it was this poem called "Just Say Yes." And I was like, "This just knocks me out. This is amazing. Let me look up this poem." It turned out she won a ton of huge awards, had an Apple documentary on her. But I didn't know her. I looked at her poem and I thought, this is great, because one of the things that I do in The Impossible Will Take a Little While is it's essays, but each major section also has a couple of poems, because somehow a really powerful poem can just take you to a different place and inspire you in a different way.
And so I did that. I could go on with all the pieces, but the goal was to find pieces that really spoke to the moment. And sometimes — another example — the piece that I found was not contemporary. We've seen all these assaults on colleges, high schools, what you can teach. Basically, we've got an administration that, like all dictatorial administrations, wants to control everything and wants to control what people learn, because if you control what they learn, that's gonna impact how they view the future. And my closest friend is Norwegian American, and he said, "What about the Norwegian teachers' resistance to the Nazis?" And I vaguely remembered it. And I thought, okay, let me go read about it. Let me try and find something.
And essentially, I ended up writing the piece myself, because there wasn't a single piece that worked. What you had is, when Germany occupied Norway during World War II, because the Norwegians were fellow Aryans, they sort of thought they would maybe go along with it and become allies. But they didn't. And so they ordered the teachers to join this organization that was modeled on Nazi organizations. The person running Norway — we now use the word "quisling" for a traitor, and it comes from this guy, Vidkun Quisling, who was the collaborator running Norway and had headed a Nazi organization in Norway before that. And they ordered all the youth to join the equivalent of the Hitler Youth, and they just laid out a whole program.
And the teachers said, "No, we're not gonna do that." And they're like, "Well, we have the guns, we're occupying your country, you're gonna do that." And the teachers just refused. First, they said you're gonna lose your pensions, you're gonna be fired. But if you fire all the teachers, then the kids have nowhere to go and they're just roaming around. And some of the parents were conscripted into German war work, so they had to stay home to look after the kids. So it disrupted that, and that didn't work. So they basically took them to concentration camps and forced labor camps — they called it "torture gymnastics," where they basically had to do various exercises in the snow. It was exhausting and brutal.
And they just refused. And the Nazis relented, and they basically ended up releasing all of them. And Quisling gave this just angry speech at a high school on the outskirts of Oslo where he said, "You teachers have ruined everything for me." And then he arrested the teachers who were there. And the ones who weren't there showed up the next day and said, "Well, you missed us. We gotta be arrested too." And basically, they abandoned the entire exercise. They still occupied Norway, but they stopped trying to enforce the Nazification of the schools. And I look at that, and it's really inspiring. There's sort of clear lessons for what happens when you actually resist, because we have colleges, we have high schools, we also have law firms and other organizations where the Trump folks basically said, "Cave to our will." Some of them did, others didn't.
And to me, there's just huge parallels. When you're told, "Oh, you can't do this," maybe one of the responses is, "Well, I'm sorry. We're gonna do this anyway." And the teachers signed a pledge saying that they would not violate their values and they would continue to teach the truth. So again, that was an example. What was it, 1943, something like that? So that's like 80 years ago. There's very few people who are alive even today from there. But boy, I was reading about it and watching people who researched it and writing about it, and it's like, that just feels like it's ripped from the headlines.
Stopping Trump from stealing the midterms.
ROZSA: Now I would like to discuss the midterm elections. President Trump has threatened to declare a national emergency, impose martial law, seize ballots and voting boxes, potentially use law enforcement such as ICE to intimidate voters, and engage in a number of other measures that would be downright dictatorial. What do you think people can do, drawing from the history that you discuss in your book, to stop this?
LOEB: Yeah. It's certainly been on my mind. I think it's been on everyone's mind who's paying attention, because he does want to be a dictator. This is no longer in doubt. So I think a number of things. One is, obviously, there's a lot of fights in the courts, and actually, we've won a lot of them, which is good. The lawyers and those organizations that are pushing that are really valuable, and more power to them. But that doesn't necessarily involve the rest of us. If they're gonna target the vote, they're gonna probably target it in the blue areas, which are the cities. And not just cities in blue states, but Houston and Dallas and Atlanta, as well as Detroit and all the other places, and smaller cities as well.
And so one of the things I think is really important to do is to work with elected officials — which ordinary citizens can do — and pressure to say, "Let's create a plan." Maybe what you need to do is to actually say, "We're gonna have our officials, and we even have our police force, out there protecting the vote. And if some Proud Boys show up, or ICE folks, they're gonna have a problem, because the law says that you have the right to vote." And I would even argue — I looked it up the other day — I think 11 states have state voting rights laws. The thing about a state voting rights law is that there's federal laws, but Trump can pardon people. Trump can't pardon people for violating a state law.
So it's setting up as many barriers as you can in advance against the disruption. And I think things like that are important. I think the election observers, the volunteering as poll workers, is really important, because you want people who actually know the rules and say, "I'm sorry, you are allowed to vote. Maybe you have to have a provisional ballot — probably not — but if you do, it's gonna get counted." All those kinds of things. So being involved — again, we don't have a lot of time, but getting what I'm gonna call the small-d democratic mechanisms of government involved on the side, overtly, of protecting voting rights, I think that matters. And that's something that ordinary citizens can pressure on, as well as just showing up.
And the other is swamping. I've got a piece that I've just sort of finished — I haven't quite decided where I'm gonna place it — just about the power of volunteering. Because one of the things that's true is that the cheating and the voter suppression make more difference in a close election. If the margin's big, there's just nothing they can do. It's like when people kicked out Viktor Orbán in Hungary. And I sort of talk about it in The Impossible Will Take a Little While. This was a while ago — it was like 2004. I spend a lot of time on election day. I volunteer and just, "Okay, where am I needed?" I'm just a foot soldier. So I volunteered. I live in Seattle.I was sent to one of our neighborhoods, knocked on a bunch of doors, got three people to vote. One person forgot it was election day. One person didn't know what to do with an absentee ballot that they'd had in the mail, and one needed a ride to the polls. So it was just your typical stuff — nothing to do with my knowledge of politics or experience or being a writer or any of that. Anybody else walking the same route would have had the same result. So I get three votes, and then it turns out — I was paying attention to the national stuff — that our governor's race was decided by 134 votes in a state of, I think it was, six million people. And I was like, "Whoa, I got one-fiftieth of the votes by myself." And if 50 fewer people had joined our side, it would have gone the other way. If 50 more on the other side had joined, it would have gone the other way.
And it was just this absolutely stark reminder that not only does your vote matter, but if you can spend a day or two days or a week or two weeks volunteering, you're going to get some other votes. And there's another U.S. Senate race I volunteered in that was decided by 2,000. A little bit bigger margin, but still, in a state that big, that's not a very big margin. So it's: how do you multiply your votes by knocking on doors, making phone calls, writing the volunteer letters and postcards, all that kind of stuff? And it does matter. And I was working on this, and I just looked up the data, because political scientists study this stuff, and there's actually data that basically says if you get — I think it's 100 contacts that you actually get through to — then you can get, I think it's three, I could look it up, three extra votes. So basically what I did was maybe a little bit above the normal, but it was basically in line with the results that happen when people knock on doors, make phone calls, and do the other stuff. Which is just, if enough people do it, then it changes the results.
To me, that's actually the most important thing, because if it can turn out the vote in large enough numbers, then it's much harder for the cheating — the voter suppression — to happen.
Courage versus cowardice.
ROZSA: You contrast the anticipatory obedience of law firms, universities, and corporations with ordinary people blowing whistles to warn neighbors about ICE agents. What separates those who stand up from those who fold?
LOEB: Yeah, good question. It was interesting, because the book has different sections and I do introductions, and that's from one of the introductions. In that particular section, I use Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," and he has this quote — it's famous, and I don't think famous enough, to be honest — where he says that the silence of the good people — because there are all these ministers saying, "Oh, it's too early. Go slower. Don't make trouble" — the silence of the good people is more damaging than the Ku Klux Klanner and the White Citizens Council. And I thought about that a lot when I was writing that introduction, because, as you say, the law firms that caved, the universities that caved, those other institutions — and these are huge and powerful institutions. And I think they were so afraid of — I don't know their minds, because I don't know the people inside, but from what I read about it — protecting: "Oh, we've got to preserve the institution." And I contrast that with the Norwegian teachers, or with the people who are resisting ICE. Alex Pretti was a nurse, Renee Good was an artist and poet.
People worked as baristas, people worked as social workers — just regular people. And I think — I don't know. I was gonna say they have less to lose, but everybody has a lot to lose. And I think the difference is that you can make complicated arguments to justify an action, or you can act. And what you said made me think of a story I haven't thought of in decades. I had this friend who was a resister in Nazi Germany, and he got captured. He escaped when the Allies bombed his prison, and he went into the forest, and he ended up in the United States, lived in Madison, started — I think it was a seed company or something. And there was some money, and he was giving money to projects. I remember sitting down with him — I was trying to get money for a project on a book on the peace movement. And he said, "Well, we just bought another house and we're building that, and we haven't sold the other one. Things are really tight." And then he said, "You know what? This is just important. We're gonna do it. We're gonna help." And that was his attitude. It's like, yeah, you could think of all sorts of reasons. If you're in Nazi Germany, it's wiser to not speak out. But he just — you just have to do it.
So on some level, you're saying, well, what really, at root, allows somebody to say, "We're just gonna do it"? And I think what it is is that maybe you feel human empathy. One of the interesting things about the tech lords and the Trump folks is that they're overtly saying human empathy is a disease. [laughs] And many of them claim that they're people of strong Christian faith. I don't know how you knock the stuff about empathy out of the best of the New Testament. You'd lose an awful lot. But they're just saying, "Hey, we're not connected to our fellow human beings. We have no relationship."
ROZSA: I have to interject here, because while they talk about "suicidal empathy" when it refers to groups they dislike, they often demand empathy for themselves. Trump demands empathy over his false claims of elections being stolen. Musk demands empathy when he loses hundreds of millions or more in his net worth. These individuals don't really oppose empathy. They simply want to be very exclusive about who receives it.
LOEB: Yeah, that's a good point. They wanna sever connections with other human beings, I think, but have absolute allegiance and no questioning of themselves. Is it that you're not feeling my pain about having the election stolen from me? Maybe, but it may be more: I said the election was stolen. You have to believe it because it's true. If I say it, it's true, so fall in line. I don't know. You're right, because it is some of both. Well, it's interesting, because Vance got in a fight with the Pope — I think it was before the current Pope became the Pope — where he posted something about how you're supposed to look after your family, and then maybe a little further, but then you essentially stop; you have no responsibility beyond that. And the guy who is now Pope, Prevost, said, "No, you absolutely are not understanding that correctly. It extends far further."
So I think it really is: who do we have ties with? And clearly, the hope with Minneapolis from the Trump folks was, "Hey, it's mostly a white state. They're gonna just say, 'Hey, all right, get rid of these people, no big deal.'" And instead, people said — it's an old labor phrase — "An injury to one is an injury to all." And that's the base. I think if you have solidarity, that is the key of social change. It goes back to the British right-wing prime minister Margaret Thatcher, who said, "There's no such thing as society. There are only individual families. So all you have to do is look after your family." And I would say every movement for justice says exactly the opposite: that we are all tied together. And that, to me, is a fundamental choice. Because otherwise, the far extension of "there's no relationship" is, "Hey, we're gonna save humanity by going to Mars, and if you're left behind on Earth, you're just gonna die in a wasteland, but you've gotta give us everything we need so we get our rockets to Mars." Which is not something I would have anticipated being a mainstream political argument.
Empathy for the cruel.
ROZSA: The problem there with the Mars argument that I find is that it isn't just immoral, it's also illogical. Musk and his fanboys love to talk about how we're going to go to Mars, but aside from having rockets, which I don't even think can reach Mars, Musk hasn't done any of the legwork in terms of making sure that a human colony on Mars could survive, and even if they could survive, determining that the conditions are such that life would be desirable. There are thousands of variables that he has yet to contemplate.
But I want to talk about another theme in your book, one that I'm actually going to push back against a little. You warn against rooting for the suffering of people who voted for leaders you oppose, quoting Heather Booth as saying, "When we organize with love at the center, we win." I recently interviewed a cognitive scientist from the University of Bristol, Stephan Lewandowsky, and I asked him why so many Trump supporters derive a sadistic glee from owning the libs, or from hearing about immigrants or trans people suffering. And his response, I'm going to read to you now, was: "If you look at internet trolls and their personality profiles, you find that they score very high on what's called the dark triad of personality: psychopathy, Machiavellianism, and narcissism." (I had to add the third one for him.) "The dark triad, that's what it's called. So we know that trolls take pleasure in trolling, which means getting other people upset." And he then speculated that Trump voters probably are motivated by similar factors. And then when I asked how they can demand sympathy for themselves, he responded, "Of course they want sympathy when they're in pain. It's just that they have no empathy to extend to other people." If we extend empathy to individuals who are motivated by these variables and who, on a systematic level, wish to withhold empathy from others, aren't we rewarding them? And by rewarding them, aren't we creating a culture where empathy more broadly will not be applied?
LOEB: It's a really good question. I guess I would distinguish. There's sort of different circles of power and complicity in what's happening now, in the destructive stuff. So you start with Trump and his folks, and then you go to the internet trolls and the MAGA activists, and then you go to the larger base of all the people who voted for him. And I confess that it's very hard to have empathy, sympathy, or anything else for those people at the top. They're just miserable human beings, and if they went to Mars, I'd be delighted. [laughs] Leave us alone. But the people who, from the anonymity of the web, are "Ah, gotcha, lib," and that kind of thing — they may be pretty messed-up human beings as well, and maybe some compassion. I think when I wrote that, I'm thinking more of just the very large — well, whatever the number is, the slight majority of the people who voted for Trump, many of whom now are just getting creamed by his decisions. Because of course they expected that he's gonna bring down prices, he's going to make things better, he's going to get rid of the competition and build American industrial bases — all the BS claims that he gave. And now they're getting creamed. The farmers — just killed by the tariffs. So I look at them, and there's sort of two ways to respond. And I would admit that in some moments I think, huh, that'll teach them.
I think many of us do that. "You thought he was gonna keep us out of wars; look at what we got now." But then I sort of step back, and I use this wonderful Alice Walker piece where she uses an ancient curse collected by Zora Neale Hurston — it was sort of collected folklore — like, their children will wither and their crops will starve. It's just bitter, bitter, bitter. And then she says, "Yeah, I'm really tempted, because maybe we mess things up. Maybe everybody just deserves to — let's start over with some other species." And then she says, on the other end, there are these moments of human courage, there's the richness.
It's interesting, I think two different people in the book mention fresh peaches. And as we're talking right now, the end of the season for peaches has just about happened [laughs], and then we're gonna have to wait a while. But man, there is nothing like a fresh peach. And that's a gift. So it takes us out of the bitterness, remembering, God, there's a world with fresh peaches in it. So I think for those trolls, it's not as if we have to sort of defer to them and spend our lives feeling sorry for them. But the notion that says, "All right, they've been prevailing; now we'll just stomp them" — I think it just leads into a trap.
Again, in the book, one of the closing sections, old and new version, is Desmond Tutu talking about the Truth and Reconciliation Commission in South Africa. And there you really did have a whole white population — with some super honorable, courageous exceptions — but the majority was super complicit in a brutal regime, which they derived in part from our brutal regime in the U.S., in segregation and Jim Crow. So how do you deal with that? What they did was they wanted to tell the story. So they said, basically, people would get amnestied for their participation in essentially human rights crimes under apartheid if they told the entire story, didn't hold back, really made it clear. And what it did is it brought the story to the surface. And it meant that the country, to some degree, grappled with its past — certainly in a way that we've never done, racially at least. And I think it had a beneficial effect. It's not to say South Africa's perfect, but if you ask how do you live together after a majority of the population is complicit in a moral — I think that helped. And he was suggesting it for Rwanda, where there had been those horrible massacres. So I don't think it's an easy question. But my sense is you've gotta, A, obviously live together with folks who you don't agree with politically. And you also have to not write huge swaths of people out of humanity, because I think that ends up feeding that kind of cycle.
And I'm not saying it's easy to do, because, my God, I've had those impulses, and I just look and I think, "Hey, good. They got creamed. They deserve it." But the "they got creamed" is probably not mostly the internet trolls. It's just these people who are trying to get by and voted — believed some lies, believed some propaganda. And they're really different from the Trumps and the Stephen Millers and those kinds of folks.
There's a quote from Abraham — the great rabbi and civil rights ally A.J. Heschel. He said, "We're not all equally guilty, but we are equally responsible." We all are responsible. We all have to do something, but some of us are more guilty and others of us aren't.

item.title: Dancing in the dark: Mousing on the upper Delaware River at night is a tradition all its own
item.description: This article describes the unique experience of night fishing for trout on the Delaware River with a guide, focusing on the sensory and emotional aspects of the activity.
item.content:encoded:
Cross Current Outfitters guide Bill Longstreet has been sticking to a keto diet as of late. I learn this while he shares his pickled eggs form Preston’s Market with me.
We are anchored in a popular dry-fly pool on the upper Delaware’s west branch in complete darkness.
“Here,” Longstreet says.
I pause from throwing an 8-weight rod with a short 20-pound Maxima leader clinched to a mouse imitation and click on the red light of my headlamp.
“Don’t worry,” Longstreet reassures me as he hands me another egg. “I have plenty of wet wipes.”
There is an anxiety fermenting, and although I’m momentarily comforted by the reassurance Longstreet has just offered, an alternative anxiety grows out of the fact that we are chasing fish that are also on a keto diet.
“Did you hear that,” Longstreet asks.
It sounds like someone is throwing rocks into the river from high up on the bank, but the noises we are hearing are big brown trout cruising the pool and every so often leaving the water to kill their meal as hard as they possibly can. Longstreet thinks they are still feeding on a spinner fall long after dusk. That or small mammals paddling across the surface.
If typical dry fly fishing is the classical music that plays behind the long, storied montage of the upper Delaware River, then mousing at night for large, nocturnal trout is very much the punk rock. In appearance, Longstreet is at least a rod length from Beethoven or Johnny Ramone, but like a good wedding band he covers it all.
That’s not to say that there isn’t skill involved in casting at night for trout, but there is far less technicalities than presenting a dry fly to a rising fish during an evening hatch.
Chasing trout in the dark is in vogue, perhaps a tradition all to itself, and needless to say this river is full of traditions. Right on the edge of the Catskills, it is a watershed that holds immense weight for fly fishing culture in the east.
As a testament to that sentiment, there are plenty of people still soaking in the water, even at this hour. Down river from us, a head lamp flashes along the shore, someone just wrapping up their evening it seems. We drift past Mike, who is wading in the middle of the pool, waist deep, smoking a pipe. I can see the embers glowing in the bowl. The sweet scent of tobacco reminds me of my grandfather, who used to smoke Half-And-Half. We trade salutations.
